lines.title: HOOK
lines.headline: A TWENTIETH OF A PIXEL
lines.narration_text: Say you want a galaxy's speed to within one kilometer per second, using only its light. You have to find a line of color to a twentieth of a pixel. The pixel that catches that light is more than twenty times wider. So how can a ruler read a mark that fine?
lines.visual_intent: pixel row, empty; 1 km/s = 0.0022 nm; pixel = 0.05 nm = 23x wider; bracket: one whole pixel; 1/20 of a pixel?; the tiny mark inside the pixel; can a ruler read it?; ring round the tiny mark; how?

lines.title: HOW LIGHT GIVES A SPEED
lines.headline: COLOR TO SPEED
lines.narration_text: Here is how light gives you a speed. Hydrogen gives off light at one exact color, six hundred fifty-six point two eight nanometers. If a galaxy moves away from us, that color stretches a little. If it moves toward us, it squeezes. The size of the change is the speed.
lines.visual_intent: pixel row (carried); hydrogen: 656.28 nm; marker: line at lab position; away: color stretches; toward: color squeezes; size of change = speed; shift / 656.28 nm = speed / light speed; bigger shift = faster galaxy

lines.title: SETUP
lines.headline: ONE LINE, ONE ROW
lines.narration_text: I'm Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI. I didn't use a telescope. I built the measurement: a line of hydrogen light, and a row of pixels. Photons fall in one at a time, and all I see is which pixel caught each one.
lines.visual_intent: pixel row (carried); Tanmay Kulkarni - Humanitarians AI; no telescope: simulated; hydrogen line shape; photons fall one at a time; photons: 1

zones.text: photons fall one at a time

lines.title: TEN
lines.headline: TEN PHOTONS
lines.narration_text: Ten photons. I guess where the center of the line is, and I am off by about fifteen kilometers per second. That is most of a pixel. With ten photons, I know almost nothing.
lines.visual_intent: pixel row (carried); photons: 6 counting up to 10; best guess marker; 15 km/s off; most of a pixel; almost nothing known

lines.title: THE TURN
lines.headline: A THOUSAND PHOTONS
lines.narration_text: A hundred photons, and my guess steadies. A thousand, and I am off by only one point four, about six percent of a pixel. Notice what did not happen. The pixel never got smaller. The guess got finer.
lines.visual_intent: pixel row (carried); photons: 100; guess steadies; photons: 1,000; 1.4 km/s off = 6% of a pixel; error bracket against one pixel; pixel: unchanged; guess: 16x finer than the pixel

lines.title: WHY
lines.headline: THE RULE
lines.narration_text: Why? Every photon is a small vote for where the center is, and votes average out. The error is the width of the line, divided by the square root of the photons. So a hundred times the light buys ten times the precision.
lines.visual_intent: pixel row (carried); each photon = one vote; votes average out; the spread of votes narrows; error = width / sqrt(photons); x100 light = x10 precision; checked: 10 to 100,000 photons; ring round the rule

lines.title: THE LIMIT
lines.headline: THE LIMIT
lines.narration_text: I want to be honest about what this is. It is a simulated line. Add ten times as much sky glow as light from the line, and my error more than doubles. I did not test blended neighbors or instrument error, and I measured nothing on a telescope.
lines.visual_intent: pixel row (carried); simulated line only; clean: 1.4 km/s; 10x sky glow: 3.4 km/s; sky glow: tested; ring round 1.4 to 3.4 km/s; not tested: blends, instrument error; telescope data: none; error: 2.3x bigger

lines.title: CLOSE
lines.headline: Reading a Twentieth of a Pixel
lines.narration_text: So the next time you see a speed quoted that finely, ask how many photons paid for it. The long film works through the numbers. It is called Reading a Twentieth of a Pixel.
